title: HTTP resilience
description: Runtime-neutral TypeScript retry with exponential backoff and full jitter, AbortSignal-aware timeouts, an idempotency-safe Fetch retry wrapper that honors Retry-After, and an in-process circuit breaker.

notes: Requires a TypeScript build and the Fetch standard (Request, Response, Headers, ReadableStream), AbortController/AbortSignal, DOMException, and setTimeout: Node.js 22+, Bun, Deno, Cloudflare Workers, Next.js route handlers, and Hono handlers on those runtimes.
Written against Web Platform APIs only; also loads in modern browsers, but the repository tests run on Node.js only and the module is declared for server use.
No runtime packages, environment reads, timers, or network activity occur at install or import time.

configuration: retry: attempts (1–20, total including the first call), baseDelayMs, maxDelayMs (0–3600000), jitter "full" (default) or "none", optional shouldRetry(error, attempt) returning boolean or { delayMs }, signal, and injectable sleep/random.
withTimeout(fn, ms, signal?): ms 1–3600000; fn receives the combined signal.
fetchWithRetry(fetch, input, init, options): attempts default 3, baseDelayMs, maxDelayMs, jitter, optional attemptTimeoutMs, signal (defaults to init.signal), injectable sleep/random/now.
createCircuitBreaker: failureThreshold (1–1000 consecutive counted failures), resetAfterMs (1–86400000), optional clock and isFailure(error).
limitations: fetchWithRetry retries only GET/HEAD/OPTIONS/PUT/DELETE or requests carrying an Idempotency-Key header; supplying that header is the caller's assertion that the server deduplicates. PUT/DELETE are idempotent by HTTP semantics, not by every server's implementation.
ReadableStream request bodies are never replayed (sent once). Request inputs are cloned per attempt, which buffers their body in memory.
Retry-After values above maxDelayMs are capped, not obeyed; the request is retried sooner than the server asked. Lower attempts or treat the response as final if that is unacceptable.
Network-error detection treats TypeError and TimeoutError as retryable; non-standard Fetch implementations that throw other error types are not retried.
withTimeout stops waiting on abort but cannot stop work that ignores its signal.
The circuit breaker is in-process state only; it is not shared across processes, isolates, or serverless instances. Retries add load; combine with server-side rate limits and budgets.
Tests use injected sleep/clock/random and a fake Fetch boundary; no live network calls were made.
